seoTitle: Investment Calculator - Calculate ROI and Future Value
metaDescription: Free investment calculator. Estimate your future wealth, compound interest, and return on investment (ROI) based on initial deposits and regular contributions.
intro: Planning for the future starts with understanding how your money can grow over time. Whether you are saving for retirement, a down payment on a house, or just building wealth, our free Investment Calculator helps you project the future value of your portfolio. By factoring in your initial investment, regular monthly contributions, expected rate of return, and the time horizon, this tool gives you a clear picture of your financial trajectory and the incredible power of compound growth.
whatIs: An investment calculator is a financial tool designed to forecast the future value of an investment over a specific period. It uses the principles of compound interest to show how the money you invest today, plus any ongoing contributions, will grow when the returns themselves earn returns. It is an essential planning tool for investors wanting to set realistic goals and determine how much they need to save to reach them.
howToUse: Enter your Initial Investment (the amount of money you are starting with).
Enter your Monthly Contribution (the amount you plan to add each month).
Input your expected Annual Return Rate (the average percentage you expect to earn).
Input the Investment Length in years.
Click 'Calculate' to see your projected future balance, total contributions, and total interest earned.
howItWorks: The calculator uses the compound interest formula for both the principal and the series of regular deposits (an annuity). The formula for the future value of the principal is P(1 + r/n)^(nt), and the formula for the future value of a series of contributions is PMT × {[(1 + r/n)^(nt) - 1] / (r/n)}. The tool combines these two formulas, compounding the returns (typically annually or monthly) to give you the total projected value.
workedExample: Suppose you start with $10,000, contribute $500 every month, and expect an annual return of 7% over 20 years. Your total contributions will be $130,000 ($10,000 + $500 × 240 months). Thanks to compounding, your total interest earned will be $171,940. Your final investment balance after 20 years will be $301,940. You more than doubled your total out-of-pocket money!
resultInterpretation: Your results are broken down into Total Future Value (the final balance), Total Contributions (the money you actually put in), and Total Interest/Earnings (the money your money made). A larger portion of earnings compared to contributions indicates that compounding has done the heavy lifting. The chart or breakdown will typically show exponential growth in the later years.
useCases: Retirement Planning: Estimate how much your 401(k) or IRA will be worth when you retire.
Goal Setting: Figure out how much you need to save monthly to reach a specific financial target (e.g., $1 million).
Comparing Scenarios: See the difference in outcomes if you save $300 a month vs. $500 a month.
Understanding Compounding: Visualize how starting to invest 10 years earlier drastically changes the final amount.
tipsAndLimitations: The expected rate of return is an estimate. Stock markets fluctuate, and historical returns (like the S&P 500's average of 7-10%) do not guarantee future performance.
Inflation reduces purchasing power. A 7% return in a 3% inflation environment means your real return is roughly 4%.
Taxes and investment fees are typically not included in basic calculations but will reduce your actual take-home returns.
Consistency is key. Regular monthly contributions often have a bigger impact on your final balance than trying to time the market.

faq.question: What is a good rate of return to use?
faq.answer: For diversified stock market portfolios over long periods, many financial planners use 6% to 8% as a conservative estimate of annual returns before inflation.

faq.question: How does compound interest work?
faq.answer: Compound interest means you earn returns on your initial money PLUS you earn returns on the returns you've already made. Over time, this creates exponential growth.

faq.question: Should I adjust for inflation?
faq.answer: Yes, to understand your future purchasing power, you can either subtract the expected inflation rate from your return rate (e.g., 8% return - 3% inflation = 5% real return) or mentally discount the final number.
